title: Vector Databases Too Expensive — AWS S3 Vector Might Be Your Answer
partialText:
Background

In my previous articles, I have shared quite a bit about RAG systems. One of the most important components in any RAG pipeline is vector storage. High-performance vector databases are usually expensive. But what if you need to store massive amounts of vector data, and latency is not your top priority? Can we find a balance between performance and cost? And if so, what storage option fits that trade-off?

That is exactly where AWS S3 Vector comes in. In this article, I will share what I learned about this service and walk you through a hands-on example.

After reading this post, you should understand how S3 Vector extends the S3 object storage model to vector data, and how to use it in a simple RAG-style workflow.

From S3 to S3 Vector

Characteristics of S3 Object Storage

Among the three major storage types — object storage, block storage, and file storage — S3 is the classic example of object storage. Unlike the other two, S3 stores data as objects inside a flat container (in S3, this container is called a Bucket). Each object contains a key (name), data content, and metadata. The structure looks roughly like this:

Bucket
  └── Object (key → file/blob + metadata)

Because of this design, S3 offers several advantages:

  • Extremely strong scalability
  • Very low cost for massive, infrequently modified data

Of course, it also has limitations, such as:

  • Not ideal for frequent random read/write operations — you work at the whole-object level
  • Relatively higher latency

That is why AWS S3 (or Azure Blob Storage) is a great fit for backups, media files, logs, and other static data scenarios. In more complex architectures, S3 often works alongside high-performance storage services to form a hot/cold multi-tier storage design.

In the AI era, this same pattern naturally extends to vector storage.

How S3 Vector Extends S3

From a product positioning perspective, S3 Vector solves the same problem that S3 solved in the traditional cloud era: store more data at a lower cost. The difference is that the data being stored is vector data.

Of course, you could store raw semantic vectors directly in a classic S3 Bucket. But for AI applications, raw vector data alone is not very useful. What we actually need is similarity search over vectors — the foundation for building Agents or RAG systems.

So S3 Vector keeps the familiar Bucket concept and introduces a new storage structure on top of it:

Vector bucket
  └── Vector index
        └── Vector (key → embedding + metadata)

The key difference is that S3 Vector introduces an index layer, where embeddings and metadata are stored as key-value pairs.

You can still read an embedding by key, but in real AI applications, what you usually need is to search for information that is semantically closest to a query.

That is the biggest difference from a classic S3 Bucket. Beyond storage, S3 Vector also manages underlying compute resources in a Serverless way. When a user query comes in, the service performs the search for you.

This Serverless, pay-as-you-go compute model means resources are triggered only when APIs are accessed — not kept running while idle. That keeps compute costs as low as possible.

Smart design, right? It is a strong fit for scenarios with massive vector storage, moderate access volume, and relaxed latency requirements — very much aligned with the design philosophy of object storage.

Next, let’s walk through a simple example to see how S3 Vector works in practice.

Demo

Create a Vector Bucket

As you can see, S3 Vector has its own dedicated client:

import boto3
session = boto3.Session()
region = session.region_name
# Create a S3 Vectors client in the AWS Region of your choice.
s3vectors = boto3.client("s3vectors", region_name=region)
bedrock = boto3.client("bedrock-runtime", region_name=region)
# Create a vector bucket
s3vectors.create_vector_bucket(vectorBucketName="media-embeddings")

The created Vector Bucket looks like this:

Create a Vector Index

Next, let’s create a Vector Index inside the Vector Bucket:

# Create a vector index "movies" in the vector bucket "media-embeddings" with non-filterable metadata keys
s3vectors.create_index(
    vectorBucketName="media-embeddings",
    indexName="movies",
    dimension=1024,
    distanceMetric="cosine",
    dataType="float32",
    metadataConfiguration={"nonFilterableMetadataKeys": ["source_text"]}
)
  • dimension and dataType define the vector dimension and numeric type. These must match the embedding model you use later.
  • distanceMetric defines how vector distance is calculated. Since we are working with plain text in this article, cosine is a good choice.
  • metadataConfiguration controls metadata behavior. By default, metadata fields support filtering. But some fields are not ideal for filtering — for example, the original source text. That field is mainly there to provide context so you know what the search result actually is. So we mark source_text as non-filterable.

The Vector Index details look like this:

Embedding and Data Ingestion

Now we can ingest data. First, we choose amazon.titan-embed-text-v2:0 as our embedding model.

Then we call put_vectors to write embedding data into the index:

import json
# Texts to convert to embeddings.
texts = [
    "Star Wars: A farm boy joins rebels to fight an evil empire in space",
    "Jurassic Park: Scientists create dinosaurs in a theme park that goes wrong",
    "Finding Nemo: A father fish searches the ocean to find his lost son"
]
# Generate vector embeddings.
embeddings = []
for text in texts:
    response = bedrock.invoke_model(
        modelId="amazon.titan-embed-text-v2:0",
        body=json.dumps({"inputText": text})
    )
    # Extract embedding from response.
    response_body = json.loads(response["body"].read())
    embeddings.append(response_body["embedding"])
# Write embeddings into vector index with metadata.
s3vectors.put_vectors(
    vectorBucketName="media-embeddings",
    indexName="movies",
    vectors=[
        {
            "key": "Star Wars",
            "data": {"float32": embeddings[0]},
            "metadata": {"source_text": texts[0], "genre": "scifi"}
        },
        {
            "key": "Jurassic Park",
            "data": {"float32": embeddings[1]},
            "metadata": {"source_text": texts[1], "genre": "scifi"}
        },
        {
            "key": "Finding Nemo",
            "data": {"float32": embeddings[2]},
            "metadata": {"source_text": texts[2], "genre": "family"}
        }
    ]
)

Pay attention to the structure of each vector entry:

{
    "key": "xxxx",
    "data": {"float32": [0.12, -0.34, ...]},
    "metadata": {"source_text": "xxxx", "genre": "xxx"}
}

Notice that float32 matches the type we defined when creating the index. The source_text field will not support filtering, while other metadata fields will.

Query and Search

As mentioned above, S3 Vector is more often used for similarity search via query_vectors, rather than reading an embedding by key.

# Query text to convert to an embedding.
input_text = "adventures in space"
# Generate the vector embedding.
response = bedrock.invoke_model(
    modelId="amazon.titan-embed-text-v2:0",
    body=json.dumps({"inputText": input_text})
)
# Extract embedding from response.
model_response = json.loads(response["body"].read())
embedding = model_response["embedding"]
# Query vector index with a metadata filter.
response = s3vectors.query_vectors(
    vectorBucketName="media-embeddings",
    indexName="movies",
    queryVector={"float32": embedding},
    topK=3,
    filter={"genre": "scifi"},
    returnDistance=True,
    returnMetadata=True
)
print(json.dumps(response["vectors"], indent=2))

We also added a metadata filter on the genre field. The final result looks like this:

[
  {
    "distance": 0.7918924689292908,
    "key": "Star Wars",
    "metadata": {
      "source_text": "Star Wars: A farm boy joins rebels to fight an evil empire in space",
      "genre": "scifi"
    }
  },
  {
    "distance": 0.8599859476089478,
    "key": "Jurassic Park",
    "metadata": {
      "genre": "scifi",
      "source_text": "Jurassic Park: Scientists create dinosaurs in a theme park that goes wrong"
    }
  }
]

Great, right? With just a few API calls, we get semantic search plus metadata filtering — a practical building block for cost-sensitive RAG systems.

Summary

S3 Vector combines S3’s low-cost storage with Serverless vector search. It is a strong option for building cost-sensitive RAG systems — especially when you have large volumes of vector data, moderate query traffic, and relaxed latency requirements.

As I mentioned in my previous RAG articles, choosing the right vector store is always a trade-off. If your workload does not need millisecond-level retrieval on every query, S3 Vector is worth a closer look.

I am Chris Bao, a software engineer focused on Azure and AWS AI platforms, specializing in AI services and Agent development on both clouds.

I offer training and consulting for enterprises and individuals. For collaboration, please contact: baoqger@gmail.com

title: 5 Reasons Why Your Talent Acquisition Strategy is Failing and How AI Can Fix It
partialText:
The United States job market is suffering not only from talent shortages but also from a widening confidence gap among employers who overestimate their ability to find suitable candidates.

According to a recent survey conducted by Robert Half, of more than 250 small business leaders in the US, 76% of respondents expressed confidence in their hiring outlook for the year ahead, but as many as 47% claimed that finding skilled talent is more difficult compared to one year ago.

To make matters more troubling, just 12% of business leaders suggested that they have the talent needed to complete high-priority projects.

Challenges are blighting talent acquisition strategies domestically through a mixture of inefficient processes, poor data utilization, and a failure to engage modern job seekers appropriately.

Employers also still grapple with age-old issues linked to human bias and manual administrative burdens, which also create problems in talent acquisition. But there’s some hope in how emerging technologies like AI are helping to tackle these problems in an effective way.

With this in mind, let’s take a deeper look at five reasons why your talent acquisition strategy might be failing and how artificial intelligence is helping to solve the problem:

1. Candidates Don’t Have a Positive Experience

When it comes to small businesses, the recruitment process for candidates can be disjointed, to say the least. This tends to be because startups and smaller companies don’t have the resources available to support a positive journey. As a result, many firms herd candidates through third-party career sites and lengthy forms.

This can result in abandoned applications, as top talent opts for more streamlined job listings instead, where they can apply for more roles in a shorter span of time.

However, artificial intelligence is helping to tackle this talent acquisition challenge with the help of text-to-apply tools and conversational AI assistants that can engage candidates instantly.

These platforms can then answer basic questions, verify minimum qualification requirements, and capture candidate data in a matter of seconds, rather than many minutes.

2. You’re Too Local

When you’re struggling to bridge skill gaps, one of the biggest traps you can fall into is recruiting for an in-house role when remote talent can carry out the duties you need just as easily.

Opening the door to remote work means accessing talent pools that can branch out nationwide and even internationally, and AI is supporting the onboarding process when it comes to matters like regional compliance and taxation laws.

Machine learning (ML) has proven to be an exceptional supporting act for adding workers in different states or countries to your payroll, monitoring around-the-clock minimum wage requirements, laws on hours worked, and state regulations to avoid costly noncompliance fees.

Artificial intelligence has also been an excellent innovation for stronger Employer of Record (EOR) visibility for employers, and Remote People, an EOR platform that has a presence in more than 150 countries, has developed its own AI Command Center, which helps to provide a holistic view of payroll, leave, and compliance for remote workers, even if they’re based on the other side of the world.

3. You’re Too Slow to Hire

The average time to hire is growing in the United States, almost doubling from 36 to 44 days in 2023 to between 63 and 68 days in 2026, and this has been a major pain point for all parties when it comes to successful hiring.

With top candidates typically remaining on the market for less than 10 days, factors such as manual interview scheduling and slow screening loops are causing more businesses to lose momentum when hiring talented staff.

Machine learning, however, can work to quickly bypass possible scheduling conflicts by allocating interview time slots when all relevant staff are free. In this dynamic, the candidates can pick their own slots allocated by ML to ensure that there are no wasteful back-and-forths through emails, shrinking the time to hire.

4. You’re Biased

Unconscious bias is a major drawback when it comes to recruitment, and it can be extremely difficult to overcome in any meaningful way.

Interviewers regularly fall victim to affinity bias, where they’re more likely to pick candidates with similar backgrounds, schools, or interests. This risks limiting workforce innovation and can make a mess of your DEI benchmarks.

Artificial intelligence solutions can lean on natural language processing (NLP) to identify and redact personal information on CVs to leave only the most important information for fair vetting processes. The type of data that can be kept away from recruiters can also include names, genders, ethnicities, and graduation years for a truly unbiased experience.

5. You’re Ignoring Data

We’re blessed with a more comprehensive level of access to data than ever before, so it can be especially frustrating that experienced recruiters still ignore quality insights by letting their gut feelings take over. This lack of objectivity can not only waste your ad spend but may also cause a far higher degree of employee turnover.

Predictive analytics software can evaluate historical hiring trends as a means of highlighting which job channels consistently deliver the highest-performing and longest-retaining employees for far stronger budget management.

This can not only help you to spend your recruitment budget wisely but also shorten your time to hire, providing greater access to talented staff.

Optimizing Your Talent Acquisition

The emergence of AI is helping to improve our ability to attract and retain the best talent for our positions. By stamping out lengthy delays through preventable application hurdles and by tackling unconscious bias in a meaningful way, more businesses are improving their access to skilled employees at scale.

Looking ahead, finding the right blend of AI and human skill in your talent search will be essential for onboarding the best candidates for roles without the risk of them falling through the net, either through a convoluted application process or because they were unfairly overlooked.

Working with actionable datasets is only the start. With the help of artificial intelligence, it’s possible to gain a holistic understanding of the recruitment landscape and the talent pool available to you.

title: How to Virus Scan Express.js File Uploads Before Saving Them
partialText:
The Express.js framework doesn’t handle file uploads on its own. To get around that, many applications use Multer middleware to process uploads, often by writing files directly to disk as soon as they arrive.

That works well for a basic upload flow, but it also creates an awkward security gap when we want to scan files for threats before saving them.

With Multer’s disk storage, files get written to disk during the upload-handling step. That means if we implement virus & malware scanning afterward in our route logic, we end up scanning files that’ve already been saved.

And that’s very bad practice in application security.

It’s a much better idea to temporarily hold uploaded files hostage in memory, then scan them, and then write them to disk after the virus & malware scan returns a clean result.

In this walkthrough, we’ll use Multer’s in-memory storage capability together with the Cloudmersive Virus Scan API to build a more secure file upload flow.

Install our dependencies

We’ll use Express.js for the route, Multer for the multipart file upload handling, and the Cloudmersive Virus Scan Node.js client for malware scanning.

npm install express multer cloudmersive-virus-api-client

Configure Multer to hold uploads in memory

We’ll first set up Multer without the disk configuration. We’ll instead use memoryStorage():

const multer = require("multer");

const upload = multer({
  storage: multer.memoryStorage(),
  limits: {
    fileSize: 10 * 1024 * 1024
  }
});

When we configure Multer this way, we get the uploaded file as a Buffer through:

req.file.buffer

Note first and foremost that nothing has been written to our upload directory yet.

You might also note that we’ve introduced a 10 MB upload limit in our example code; the goal here is just to keep memory usage predictable in this example. A 10 MB limit comfortably covers many common documents, images, business-file uploads, and so on.

Larger-file workflows would typically use a different buffering or streaming approach entirely.

Scan the uploaded file

Now we’ll pass the uploaded file buffer and original file name into Cloudmersive’s Advanced Virus Scan operation. That operation evaluates files for viruses, malware, and other threats like executables, invalid content, scripts, macros, and more.

The Node.js client exposes this through scanFileAdvanced().

Since the SDK uses a callback, we’ll wrap the API call in a Promise so we can use it with async/await:

function scanFileAdvanced(fileBuffer, originalFileName) {
  return new Promise((resolve, reject) => {
    const options = {
      fileName: originalFileName,
      allowExecutables: false,
      allowInvalidFiles: false,
      allowScripts: false,
      allowPasswordProtectedFiles: false,
      allowMacros: false,
      allowXmlExternalEntities: false,
      allowInsecureDeserialization: false,
      allowHtml: false,
      allowUnsafeArchives: false,
      allowOleEmbeddedObject: false,
      allowUnwantedAction: false
    };

    scanApi.scanFileAdvanced(
      fileBuffer,
      options,
      (error, data) => {
        if (error) {
          reject(error);
          return;
        }

        resolve(data);
      }
    );
  });
}

Note that we’re explicitly configuring our request to block a variety of content types and behaviors. If your environment explicitly allows any of these content types or behaviors, you can simply flip relevant flags (e.g., allowExecutables) to true.

In our API response, we get a simpleCleanResult flag along with some additional fields telling us why a file failed (or passed) inspection. For example, a file flagged for having executable content would return ContainsExecutable: true.

Save the file only when it passes the scan

Once the virus scan is part of our route, the important thing to focus on is the order of operations:

const scanResult = await scanFileAdvanced(
  req.file.buffer,
  req.file.originalname
);

if (scanResult.CleanResult !== true) {
  return res.status(422).json({
    message: "The uploaded file failed the security scan."
  });
}

If CleanResult is not true, the route ends before we write anything to disk.

We only create server-controlled filenames and save buffers after files pass their scans:

await fs.mkdir(uploadDirectory, {
  recursive: true
});

const storedFileName = createStoredFileName();

const destinationPath = path.join(
  uploadDirectory,
  storedFileName
);

await fs.writeFile(
  destinationPath,
  req.file.buffer
);

And that gives us the basic workflow we’re looking for. Capture uploads, hold them in memory, scan them for threats, and save them if they’re clean.

Complete route

With all those pieces together, we end up with a full route that looks like this (we’ve included some documentation for extra clarity):

const express = require("express");
const multer = require("multer");
const fs = require("fs/promises");
const path = require("path");
const crypto = require("crypto");
const CloudmersiveVirusApiClient = require(
  "cloudmersive-virus-api-client"
);

const app = express();
const port = 3000;

const uploadDirectory = path.join(__dirname, "uploads");

const upload = multer({
  storage: multer.memoryStorage(),
  limits: {
    fileSize: 10 * 1024 * 1024
  }
});

const defaultClient = CloudmersiveVirusApiClient.ApiClient.instance;
const apiKeyAuth = defaultClient.authentications["Apikey"];

apiKeyAuth.apiKey = process.env.CLOUDMERSIVE_API_KEY;

const scanApi = new CloudmersiveVirusApiClient.ScanApi();

/**
 * Scans an uploaded file using Cloudmersive Advanced Virus Scan.
 *
 * @param {Buffer} fileBuffer The uploaded file contents.
 * @param {string} originalFileName The original uploaded filename.
 * @returns {Promise<Object>} The advanced scan result.
 */
function scanFileAdvanced(fileBuffer, originalFileName) {
  return new Promise((resolve, reject) => {
    const options = {
      fileName: originalFileName,
      allowExecutables: false,
      allowInvalidFiles: false,
      allowScripts: false,
      allowPasswordProtectedFiles: false,
      allowMacros: false,
      allowXmlExternalEntities: false,
      allowInsecureDeserialization: false,
      allowHtml: false,
      allowUnsafeArchives: false,
      allowOleEmbeddedObject: false,
      allowUnwantedAction: false
    };

    scanApi.scanFileAdvanced(
      fileBuffer,
      options,
      (error, data) => {
        if (error) {
          reject(error);
          return;
        }

        resolve(data);
      }
    );
  });
}

/**
 * Creates a server-controlled filename for an approved upload.
 *
 * @returns {string} A generated storage filename.
 */
function createStoredFileName() {
  return crypto.randomUUID();
}

/**
 * Accepts one file upload, scans it, and saves it only if it is clean.
 */
app.post("/upload", upload.single("file"), async (req, res) => {
  if (!req.file) {
    return res.status(400).json({
      message: "No file was uploaded."
    });
  }

  try {
    const scanResult = await scanFileAdvanced(
      req.file.buffer,
      req.file.originalname
    );

    if (scanResult.CleanResult !== true) {
      return res.status(422).json({
        message: "The uploaded file failed the security scan."
      });
    }

    await fs.mkdir(uploadDirectory, {
      recursive: true
    });

    const storedFileName = createStoredFileName();

    const destinationPath = path.join(
      uploadDirectory,
      storedFileName
    );

    await fs.writeFile(
      destinationPath,
      req.file.buffer
    );

    return res.status(201).json({
      message: "File scanned and saved successfully.",
      fileName: storedFileName,
      verifiedFileFormat: scanResult.VerifiedFileFormat
    });
  } catch (error) {
    console.error("File scan failed:", error);

    return res.status(502).json({
      message: "The file could not be scanned."
    });
  }
});

app.listen(port, () => {
  console.log(`Server listening on port ${port}`);
});

With this implemented, we can now test the route by submitting a file with cURL:

curl -X POST \
  -F "file=@example.pdf" \
  http://localhost:3000/upload

If the file passes the advanced scan, the application returns a 201 response and writes it to the upload directory; if the file fails, the route returns 422 and skips the save step entirely.

Conclusion

Remember, the important thing here isn’t just that we scanned uploaded files for threats. That should be happening no matter what. This is about where we chose to do that in our architecture.

By keeping files in memory, we gain the ability to run our virus scan before Multer-backed content ever reaches persistent storage. That lets us block malware and other unsafe file characteristics before the application commits the file to disk.
